item.title: I run Lossless Scaling on old TV shows, and they look better than the official remasters
item.itunes:title: I run Lossless Scaling on old TV shows, and they look better than the official remasters
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You've probably heard a lot about Lossless Scaling and what it can do for older games, retro emulated titles, and games that don't support Nvidia or AMD's upscaling or frame generation technologies. By all means, it's an app that's primarily known for its frame generation layer, but part that often gets overlooked is the scaler that sits directly next to it, which can elevate how your older TV shows and movies look.

I've recently taken to upscaling my old DVD box sets using this utility, and so far, it seems to work really well when the right toggles are used. It's simple, takes about a minute, costs you just $7 to upscale anything from your digital media library, and nothing gets re-encoded, because it's all happening on your GPU.

Lossless Scaling makes a 480p source look less like a 480p source

LS1 does a surprisingly good job with anime, but so does Anime4K

The first thing I tried was Lossless Scaling's LS1 upscaler, using Dragon Ball Z: Tree of Life from a 480p DVD source. While it looks fine as it is at native, I couldn't help but notice that it got too soft on my 1440p OLED display. Anything that's animated automatically becomes an obvious candidate for Anime4K, which is designed for this specific kind of upscaling workload consisting of clean lines and flat colors, but I was curious enough to try LS1.

After a little while of noticing almost no impact on the image quality, I realized that there was a trick to getting best results out of either. Lossless Scaling tends to work with whatever VLC is rendering, rather than grabbing the video's native resolution directly. So I had to set VLC's window to the video's native size and let Lossless Scaling handle the upscaling.

With LS1 particularly, the difference wasn't night and day, but nonetheless, it was noticeable during playback. Edges got remarkably cleaner, finer details like character models seemed better defined, and of course, the footage finally arrived without some of the softness that becomes obvious when a 480p video is stretched across a 2K display.

There are, of course, limitations to this approach when the source itself is this low-resolution. Neither Anime4K nor LS1 can recover the details that don't exist in the video in the first place, and pushing 480p video to 1440p gives the algorithm a lot of empty pixels to fill in.

Lossless Scaling is what I wanted DLSS to be

DLSS may be more polished, but Lossless Scaling is what it should have evolved into

22
By  Ayush Pande

It allows me to smoothen the pace, too

LSFG makes 24fps drama easier on the eyes

When I loaded Twin Peaks: The Missing Pieces (2014) I had a slightly different approach in mind. On the 1080p Blu-ray rip, I used FSR with its sharpness slider pushed all the way up and let it handle the scaling. The result this time was a lot more subtle, but nonetheless noticeable around high-contrast edges where the extra sharpening imparted a clean, more defined appearance without looking excessively processed, as is usually the problem with upscaling from this resolution.

Now, I must confess this isn't something a lot of purists would be interested in, but I like to enable LSFG at 2x, which takes the 24fps output to 48fps. This makes camera as well as character movements a lot smoother on a 240Hz OLED screen.

I'd anticipated a lot of artefacts in the scenes that I tested, but during my 30-minute watch session, I was unable to find anything particularly off-putting. While remasters offer an image quality uplift, they can't change the original 24fps motion into something fluid. This does result in the highly unpopular soap-opera effect, though, so I understand those who do not belong to this camp and find any sort of motion smoothening on drama unwatchable.

Call me crazy, but I still use Lossless Scaling with the RTX 5090

A little extra frame generation never hurt anyone.

34
By  Jacob Roach

I'd rather upscale my shows myself than trust another AI remaster

Sometimes, keeping the original is the safer bet

There's a special reason why I would rather run this upscaling on my own GPU than wait for an official remaster, and you'd have to look no further than what Netflix did last year. In the remaster of A Different World, a 1987 sitcom, Netflix listed the show as HD, and granted, it was high-definition as promised.

Problem is, a few viewers immediately took notice of what was wrong with it. The remaster was found interspersed with visual artefacts like malformed hands, garbled text, and frequent warped faces now and then, turning the show into a classic uncanny valley nightmare.

The major problem that's associated with generative AI upscaling is the fact that it tends to predict details and patterns according to the data the specific model was trained upon, which is why something like cleaning up text in a frame becomes a gamble. You might get sharper letters, or you may end up with hieroglyphics where ordinary text used to be. The odds are overwhelmingly skewed towards the latter with most models.

Lossless Scaling's LS1, Anime4K and FSR have a far lower probability of doing anything of that sort, majorly because they are reconstruction scalers that sharpen edges that already exist. This means that finer details such as text remain soft but otherwise rather legible.

Don't give away your old DVDs just yet

While I can't promise that Lossless Scaling would turn a 480p DVD rip into a 4K remaster, it certainly can make low-resolution footage considerably easier on your 4K display, without any horrifying, immersion-breaking AI interpretations getting in the way. As such, a $7 utility and about a minute of tuning can help you revisit your old classics without waiting for a carefully AI approximated version of a remaster to come along.

item.title: Someone made their own GBA-to-Switch 2 Pokémon transferrer after Nintendo closed its official route
item.itunes:title: Someone made their own GBA-to-Switch 2 Pokémon transferrer after Nintendo closed its official route
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Hardware adapter lets a real GBA trade Pokémon directly with Switch 2 FireRed/LeafGreen
  • Provides an unofficial emergency exit to rescue GBA Pokémon once Pokémon Bank shuts down
  • No build instructions yet; an October FireRed/LeafGreen update could let these Pokémon move into Pokémon Home

A month ago, Nintendo announced that it was shutting down the Pokémon Bank service. However, it seems not everyone was ready to let go of the Game Boy era of Pokémon just yet. Someone has figured out a way to transfer Pokémon from a GBA directly to the Switch 2, without needing Nintendo's services.

This tinkerer found a way to directly bridge generations of Pokémon

It's like an emergency exit for GBA-era Pokémon

Credit: ahenley17

As spotted by Notebook Check, user ahenley17 on X posted what they've been working on. Right now, if you want to migrate a Pokémon all the way from the Game Boy Advance era to the current Switch 2 system, you need to hop from the GBA to a DS, then use the Pokémon Bank app on the DS to move the Pokémon onto the cloud, then send them over to Pokémon Home via the app, then retrieve them on your Switch 2.

The bad news is that, once Nintendo pulls the plug on Pokémon Bank, that migration route will be sealed off forever. The good news is that ahenley17 figured out a way to directly link up a GBA to their Switch 2 and send over Pokémon in a trade. All they had to do was boot up the eShop version of FireRed and LeafGreen on their Switch 2 and finagle the system into performing a trade between it and a Game Boy Advance.

Now that their Pokémon are safe on the Switch 2, they're ready to move to Pokémon Home once an update to FireRed and LeafGreen drops in October. If all goes well, they may have figured out a way to migrate Pokémon over without using Bank. They haven't listed any instructions on making your own device at home yet, so keep an eye on their space for more information.

Pokémon Red and Blue just got the HD-2D PC port I've dreamed about for years

Nintendo really should have made this happen already.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: The prototype of the game that would become Banjo-Kazooie has appeared online for preservation's sake
item.itunes:title: The prototype of the game that would become Banjo-Kazooie has appeared online for preservation's sake
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Project Dream ROM has been leaked, showing Rare's early prototype that predates Banjo-Kazooie.
  • The ROM preserves an unreleased human protagonist version before Banjo replaced the lead.
  • The leaker argues that its release aids preservation and may prompt other prototype dumps.

Personally, I love it when prototypes of games work their way online. Even if it's borderline unplayable, seeing the building blocks of what could have been, or what it would eventually be, is always fascinating to me. As such, when I heard that someone had dumped the ROM for a cancelled Rare game that would eventually spin off into Banjo-Kazooie, I knew I had to check it out; however, as it turns out, this move was more than just someone letting people play a cool beta.

The ROM for Project Dream has appeared online in a call for preservation

It's a build from before Banjo became the main character

Back in the 90s, Rare wanted to make a game that played like an RPG but used its Donkey Kong Country tech to render the graphics. The result was Project Dream, which went through a troubled development process as Rare attempted to turn its idea into a fun title. A side character called Banjo the Bear was added, who would go on to replace the main character to become the star of the show.

It seems that the ROM that was dumped online was from before this change, as it keeps the original human protagonist. However, as the leaker describes in their Internet Archive page for the game, their actions are meant to be more than just a cool insight into an early version of Banjo-Kazooie:

"But with the current state of the industry and Microsoft's current heartless gutting and mismanagement of Rare and other companies it controls, plus with how long it's been, I feel it's more important to make sure this is properly preserved, and the ROM dissected by people with far more knowledge on how to do such things.

I hope by releasing this, that it also inspires other people to release what they have as well. I know the Twelve Tales Conker 64 prototype is out there somewhere, but sadly, this is the only thing that I have."

As Rare developed Project Dream, they saw Nintendo working on its own title: the now-famous Super Mario 64. Rare knew that the game's 3D graphics would outshine Project Dream's, so it canned the game and remade it for the N64 while keeping Banjo as the main character. And just like that, you've got Banjo-Kazooie. We may never know what Project Dream may have looked like if it had been released, but given how well Banjo-Kazooie was received, scrapping the dated-looking prototype and moving to full 3D likely saved the company from a bad launch.

This fan-made Banjo-Kazooie PC port does what Nintendo won't — and it's free

Banjo: Recompiled modernizes one of my favorite childhood N64 games in the best way possible.

item.title: Proxmox wastes power by default, and the fix takes a single setting
item.itunes:title: Proxmox wastes power by default, and the fix takes a single setting
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]

I've been running Proxmox on a mini PC at home for over a year, but I never gave too much thought to how much power the PC was using. After all, I was likely going to keep it anyway.

Recently, though, I found out that Proxmox tends to waste power out of the box, and the fix is ridiculously easy. If you haven't paid attention to it before, now's the time to change this setting.

How Proxmox wastes power

CPU scaling can make a difference

Every operating system on basically any device has to determine how to use the processor inside that device according to its needs. This can often be adjusted by changing something called the governor, which changes what gets prioritized and how the processor reacts to being under load or mostly idle.

Proxmox comes with two CPU governors (though it depends on your hardware), but just from booting it up and looking around the UI, you really wouldn't know it. Out of the box, Proxmox is set to the performance governor, which enables your services to potentially run a bit faster, but causes the CPU to use more power overall. It becomes especially noticeable when you're not actively using your server, because the CPU may need to keep running faster in order to ensure maximum responsiveness when you do use it.

I optimized Proxmox's defaults and cut my home lab energy costs without sacrificing speed

Proxmox is still the best home lab OS, but its defaults are much rougher than they should be

3
By  Ayush Pande

But there's a good chance you don't actually need all the performance out of your CPU all the time. Think about it, how often do you run demanding tasks on your home lab? Mine has a few services on it, but the only one I actively access throughout the day is my self-hosted homepage, everything else is just there for when I need it. And most of those services aren't particularly demanding anyway.

That's where the other CPU governor in Proxmox, called powersave, comes into the picture. It allows the CPU to reduce power consumption more at the expense of some performance, but it's not likely I'll ever need it anyway.

Fixing it is a breeze

Community scripts do everything

Anyone who uses Proxmox should know that community scripts are the backbone of the whole ecosystem. They're usually helpful for deploying preconfigured LXCs or VMs, which run all the self-hosted services on my server, but it turns out, they can also be helpful for changing lesser-known Proxmox settings. And of course, that includes the CPU governor.

All you have to do is use the script below, which you can find on the Proxmox community scripts website:

bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/community-scripts/ProxmoxVE/main/tools/pve/scaling-governor.sh)"In Proxmox, select your homelab (under Datacenter), and then go to the Shell tab. Simply paste the command above, and you'll see what your current governor is and have the option to change it to powersave. The script also gives you the option to setup a cron job that sets the governor every time at boot, so you don't have to change it manually whenever you reboot your server.

The script doesn't just go one way, so if you happen to have a lot of services or you notice performance has dropped, you can run it again and change the governor back to performance.

I always tweak my Proxmox host's settings before spinning up a single VM or LXC

It's the only way I set up a Proxmox node now

1
By  Ayush Pande

For what it's worth, there are also more manual ways to do this using the shell if you'd rather not rely on scripts, but this is just far easier. I should also note that the options available will depend on your processor; the Intel CPU in my homelab only has these two governors, but you may have others.

Test it for yourself

Every PC is different

While this change is always worth trying, there's nothing like first-hand experience to make sure it's right for you. Some users have experienced higher CPU usage after setting the powersave governor, while others have seen significant power reductions. If you have a wattage meter, your best bet is to check what it says when using both governors so you can make sure you're saving power in the long run.

It also matters what services you're running, an how many. If you have a lot of containers and VMs on your PC and you access them frequently, the performance governor should help ensure your PC can keep up with the workload more effectively and maintain better performance.

I enable these 4 Proxmox settings on every fresh install, and most guides skip them entirely

These Proxmox optimizations saved me from overheating and catastrophic data loss

2
By  Ayush Pande

Still, I suspect a lot of people are in a similar situation to mine. If you just set up a home lab to start tinkering or you only need a couple of services, there's a good chance your CPU is working too hard and wasting power.

There are other things you can try if you're looking to save power, too. Sometimes, your PC's BIOS may also have additional settings to reduce power consumption, or it may be time to check whether you're still using the services you have constantly running. You may also consider putting your entire server to sleep when you're not using it.

Cut down on your electricity bill

Self-hosting services and storage can save you a lot of money on cloud services, but without the right settings, that money can just end up going towards your electricity bill for keeping it all running 24/7. Simple settings like these can result in real savings, so I highly recommend giving this a shot and seeing what it does for you.

item.title: Years after leaving Google Photos, the thing I miss most isn't what I expected
item.itunes:title: Years after leaving Google Photos, the thing I miss most isn't what I expected
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For years, Google Photos was the place where I kept my entire photo collection. It was one of those apps I rarely thought about because it simply worked in the background. Eventually, though, I decided I wanted a different approach and started looking for a way to manage my photos on my own terms. That led me to Immich. The switch was easier than I expected, and after using it for years, I’ve found that I don't really miss most of what I left behind. But there is one Google Photos feature I didn't realize I would notice until it was gone.

Immich replaced almost everything I cared about

The transition was easier than expected

Once I moved my library to Immich, I realized I wasn't giving up as much as I had expected. The basic experience of managing my photos felt familiar enough that I didn't spend weeks trying to adjust to a completely different workflow.

The biggest win for me was the automatic backup from my phone. I could take photos throughout the day and let Immich handle getting them onto my own server. I didn't have to remember to manually copy everything over, which was important because a backup system is only useful when you actually use it consistently.

I also liked having a proper timeline for browsing my library. Photos were arranged in a way that made it easy to move through different periods without dealing with a messy collection of folders and files. Albums were another part of my old workflow that I didn't have to abandon. I could still group photos for specific trips, events, or other occasions and access them from my devices.

I expected to miss Google Photos' search, but I don't

I found what I needed anyway

Search was one of the features I thought would make leaving Google Photos difficult. Google had years of data about my library, and I was used to typing a few words and getting surprisingly relevant results. I assumed I would notice the difference every time I needed to find an older picture.

That hasn't really happened. Immich's search is good enough for the way I actually use my library. If I'm trying to find photos from a particular trip, a certain person, or even something specific that appears in a picture, I can usually get there without much trouble. I don't always remember the exact date or album, so being able to search naturally is useful.

There are still situations where Google's search feels more polished, especially when I'm looking for something unusually specific. But those cases don't come up often enough for me to care. Most of the time, I can find what I'm looking for without much effort. That was a pleasant surprise. I expected search to be one of the biggest compromises of moving to Immich, but in everyday use, it simply hasn't been.

I self-hosted a Google Photos alternative with a Synology NAS — here's how it went

Build your own photo management platform with a NAS!

11
By  Rich Edmonds

The thing I actually miss is much harder to replace

Nothing quite replaces those unexpected memories

The feature I didn't expect to miss was Google Photos' Memories. I didn't think much about them while I was using the service because they were always there in the background. Every now and then, Google Photos would show me pictures from years ago, and I'd end up scrolling through them for a few minutes. I didn't realize how much I enjoyed that until those reminders disappeared.

The interesting thing is that these weren't necessarily my best photos. Sometimes they were completely ordinary pictures I had forgotten about. A random lunch, an old weekend outing, a picture of something I bought, or a moment with people I hadn't thought about in years could suddenly become interesting simply because I hadn't seen it for so long.

With Immich, I still have those photos. I can browse through them whenever I want, but I have to make the effort myself. There isn't the same feeling of being surprised by something from my own photo history. That's the part I genuinely miss. I don't miss another storage feature or a clever editing tool. I miss being reminded of moments I'd completely forgotten.

I still wouldn't switch back to Google Photos

The trade-off is worth it

Even with that one thing I miss, I have no plans to move my library back to Google Photos. Leaving it made me realize that I value having more control over where my photos live and how I manage them.

With Immich, I know exactly where my library is stored. I'm not depending on a third-party service to decide how my photos are handled, and I can manage the underlying storage myself. That gives me a level of control I didn't have before.

There is also something satisfying about knowing that my photo library isn't tied to a particular cloud service. I can change the hardware, adjust my setup, or move things around without having to rethink my entire workflow.

4 lessons I learned after switching from Google Photos to a self-hosted solution

It has gone better than expected, but with a few hurdles.

16
By  Megan Ellis

I traded convenience for control

Moving away from Google Photos taught me that not every convenience needs to be replaced. Some features are nice to have, but they aren't worth giving up control over something as personal as my photo library. Immich has changed how I manage my photos, and while I occasionally miss the little surprises from my old setup, I don't regret making the switch.

item.title: I retired my Roku stick for an Android TV box, and I'm not going back
item.itunes:title: I retired my Roku stick for an Android TV box, and I'm not going back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When streaming media services and devices became popular, Roku was my first choice. Even with the ability to sideload other apps on Fire TV devices, I stuck with Roku boxes and sticks since they were straightforward to use, my apps synced, and I was used to the experience.

I still had a stick until retiring it in favor of an Android TV box. The number of ads on Roku is horrendous, and the platform offers no customization. I can also do a lot more with an Android/Google TV box than with the Roku OS.

Roku lacks apps and customization options

An Android TV box offers more

While Roku has more than 40,000 apps in its store, that number still pales in comparison to the number available for Android TV. Between the official Play Store, alternative stores, and Android APKs available for sideloading from GitHub and other sources, the number of apps is in the millions.

I can instantly customize the look and feel of Google TV with a few clicks using alternative launchers such as Projectivy, Arc, or Kyu. I also have access to a plethora of ways for managing my own media. Even phone apps that don't offer a TV-like viewing experience let me get things done that I can't on Roku.

The locked-down Roku operating system leaves little room for interface customization, and it definitely doesn't allow you to remove ads. I can install themes, rearrange tiles, adjust the wallpaper, or change the screensaver, but the same blocky interface with the same ad annoyances always remains; just with a theme around it.

For instance, I installed a Game of Thrones theme thinking it would revitalize my Roku, but it did nothing more than change the wallpaper and put borders around the blocky app tiles. item.title: I built Claude Code's workflow with a local model, and it's surprisingly close
item.itunes:title: I built Claude Code's workflow with a local model, and it's surprisingly close
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Claude Code can inspect a repository, read and edit files, run terminal commands, and check whether its changes actually work. The model plays a huge role here, of course, but much of the experience comes from the workflow built around it. I wanted to see whether I could recreate that workflow while keeping the model on my own computer. I combined Qwen 3.5 with LM Studio and Hermes Agent. I’m running the 14B model, so it’s nowhere near as good as Claude, but this setup brought me pretty close to what I had in mind, with a few limitations, of course.

LM Studio runs the model

Hermes handles the actual work

LM Studio loads Qwen 3.5 on my computer and makes it available through an OpenAI-compatible API. I previously used Ollama, but I prefer LM Studio because it doesn’t force me to use the command line all the time, and its Hugging Face integration comes in handy. To run the agent, I use Hermes, which connects to that API instead of using LM Studio’s chat interface. While I prefer Hermes, you can use another tool, such as OpenCode or even Claude Code. OpenAI’s Codex also supports local models.

Hermes Agent provides the tools Qwen needs to work inside a project. These include functions for searching, reading, patching, and writing files, along with terminal access for running commands. When Qwen requests a tool, Hermes executes it and sends the output back to the model. For example, a coding request can move from search_files to read_file, then to patching the relevant file and running a test command, without me copying code between a chat window and an editor.

Of course, this setup isn’t as convenient as Claude Code, which packages the entire workflow into one product. My version splits it into three components: Qwen decides what to do, LM Studio runs the model, and Hermes carries out the actions. But given that none of this costs me anything, I’m happy to keep using it.

Your CLAUDE.md is probably wrong, and here's how Anthropic's engineers actually structure theirs

Your file is probably doing more harm than good

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Getting the local workflow running

You can spin this up in minutes

Qwen 3.5’s 14B model runs on my M5 MacBook Pro with 24GB of unified memory. I used a 4-bit quantized build and limited the context window to 32,768 tokens, which left enough memory for macOS, Hermes, and any terminal commands running alongside the model.

LM Studio can expose a loaded model through an OpenAI-compatible server. You can start it from the Developer tab, after which the model becomes available at http://localhost:1234/v1. Hermes includes LM Studio as a provider, so I only had to select it through hermes model and choose the Qwen model already loaded in memory.

Hermes’ coding toolset provides file search, editing, terminal access, memory, and task planning. An AGENTS.md file can also tell the agent how your project is organized, which build commands to use, and what checks it should run after changing code. Mine requires Hermes to inspect existing files before editing them and run the relevant tests afterward.

Command approvals are worth keeping enabled when the agent runs directly on your computer. I used Hermes’ smart approval mode, limited file access to the project directory, and worked from a separate Git branch, so a bad edit wouldn’t affect the main copy.

It works best when the job stays focused

Though the experience isn’t the same as Claude Code

Focused coding jobs gave me the closest experience to Claude Code. I tested the agent with a configuration bug that caused the project to ignore a user-defined setting. Qwen searched for references to the setting, inspected the configuration loader, changed the relevant file, and ran the existing tests through Hermes.

The first patch caused a fallback test to fail. Qwen read the terminal output, adjusted the condition it had added, and ran the test suite again. I didn’t have to identify the file or paste the error back into the conversation. Each step took longer than it would with Claude Code, though, especially when Qwen had to process several files or a large terminal response.

You'll start seeing the limits of the 32K context window once you ask for bigger changes. You can ask Hermes to compress the conversation, but some earlier details will disappear in the process. A better approach here is to split a feature into smaller requests. Qwen also produces an invalid tool call at times, which can stop the workflow until you repeat the request.

Local agents are getting better

Local agents are much better than they were a few years ago. Now, if you have a decent machine, such as a MacBook Pro or even a MacBook Air with more than 16GB of RAM, you can run a very good model that can do a lot for you for free. If you have a machine with a dedicated GPU and enough VRAM, you can even run something like a 32-billion-parameter model. Paired with a tool such as Hermes, it can produce output worth considering.

I switched from Claude Code to Codex for a week, and the trade-offs surprised me

One week, two tools, a lot of opinions.

item.title: I moved my most important devices off Wi-Fi, and my entire network became more reliable
item.itunes:title: I moved my most important devices off Wi-Fi, and my entire network became more reliable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I was using Wi-Fi for far more than I should have. If a device could connect wirelessly, I usually let it, even when it sat in the same place every single day. My desktop, Apple TV, NAS, game console, and other important devices were all using the airtime for no good reason. Then I stopped treating Wi-Fi as the default.

I didn’t buy a new router, upgrade to Wi-Fi 7, or change my internet plan, yet my entire network felt more stable almost immediately.

I ran my home server on Wi-Fi for a year, and learned when Ethernet actually matters

Wired connections might be 'best' but sometimes just enough is fine

22
By  Joe Rice-Jones

I realized my most demanding devices didn’t need Wi-Fi

I was wasting Wi-Fi on stationary devices

My most demanding devices were the ones that moved the least. My Apple TV 4K sits in the same spot under the TV every day, and my Windows desktop never leaves my desk. Yet I was still letting both of them use Wi-Fi as if they needed the flexibility of a wireless connection.

That didn’t make much sense once I thought about it. These are also two of the busiest devices on my network. The Apple TV 4K regularly handles 4K streaming, while my desktop deals with large downloads, cloud backups, file transfers, local LLM updates, video calls, and plenty of other bandwidth-heavy tasks.

I was basically asking Wi-Fi to handle some of my heaviest traffic, even though both devices were sitting just a few feet away from an Ethernet connection.

So I changed the setup. I connected both devices directly to Ethernet and left Wi-Fi for the gadgets that actually benefit from it, such as phones, tablets, laptops, and smart home devices.

4K streaming became much more predictable

My Windows desktop benefited even more

The biggest difference with my Apple TV 4K wasn’t some dramatic jump in speed. It was consistency. Before switching to Ethernet, streaming was generally good, but there were occasional moments where playback took longer to start, quality dipped briefly, or the connection felt less noticeable once I wired it.

4K content now starts more predictably and stays steady even when other devices are active. I just want to press play and forget about the network.

My Windows desktop benefited even more because it does far more than stream content. Some of the bandwidth-heavy jobs can run for a long time and keep the connection busy in the background. item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Amazon Fire HD 10 is a bestselling tablet for several reasons. It isn't for everyone, but the price will surely turn heads if you've been thinking about buying a new Android tablet. Amazon is now discounting the Fire HD 10 to just $77, which is 50% off its usual retail price of $155.

Amazon Fire HD 10

The Fire HD 10 is one of the best Fire tablets available with its large display, updated internals, and access to apps, videos, games, and more. 

See at Amazon

A perfect fit for some

Credit: Amazon

If this tablet fits your daily flow, it's worth picking up. It's just that simple. The tablet features a 10.1-inch screen, octa-core processor, 4GB of RAM, and 32GB of onboard storage. It also has a microSD card slot, so you can expand storage if needed.

Although it runs Android, it is a special version created by Amazon, which means it doesn't have access to the Google Play Store. However, Amazon has its own App Store that provides access to some of the most popular Android apps right now.

It doesn't have every app available that you'd find on the Google Play Store, but it's good enough. If you have specific needs, double-check whether your app can be downloaded to the Fire HD 10.

And despite its lower price, this tablet charges via USB-C. Plenty of accessories are also available to make it more productive. I've used one before, and it got me by when I just needed something to listen to music, watch videos, and browse the web.

item.title: Nvidia's biggest ray tracing leap in years is free for every RTX GPU, and 3 games on my RTX 40-series have never looked this good
item.itunes:title: Nvidia's biggest ray tracing leap in years is free for every RTX GPU, and 3 games on my RTX 40-series have never looked this good
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction was finally unveiled at Gamescom, putting the finishing touch on what could only be described as one of the most remarkable leaps in upscaling technology that is Nvidia's second-generation transformer-based DLSS 4.5 stack. Unlike many GPU features that arrive with a new generation of hardware attached, this one comes as a free present for all GeForce RTX graphics card owners.

Ray Reconstruction combines upscaling and denoising into a single model, which means Nvidia gets to tackle two of the most pressing problems in rendering with the same technology. The new model is now available as Preset F in the Nvidia App, replacing the DLSS 4.0-era Preset D, and it works across every RTX generation from Turing onward.

Curious to see what this means for GPUs that aren't Blackwell-class, I put Preset F and Preset D head-to-head on my humble RTX 4070 Ti Super, testing both image quality and performance at 1440p across three games to see what Team Green has promised, and what they have delivered.

The test bench for the runs detailed below comprised of a GeForce RTX 4070 Ti Super coupled with a Ryzen 5 7600X, with 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory running with EXPO enabled.

Resident Evil Requiem

DLSS 4.5 RR brings a requiem for noisy reflections

Nvidia states that the new Ray Reconstruction model should bring better lighting accuracy, stronger temporal stability, and clearer detail in ray-traced scenes all while maintaining roughly the same performance as the preceding model. With Resident Evil Requiem, there are a couple of challenges involved in showing all of that off, though. Much of the game is characterized by dimmer lighting, matte concrete, and in a specific reflective scene that I captured under both presets, the two come quite close, barring the obvious clarity and crispiness in reflections.

Which is why I'd argue the gains become easier to spot when you put Preset F in front of reflections. Wet floors in the same dimly lit areas have more convincing color and reflection, and the lighting looks brighter and better defined. Pushing the brightness too far, in my testing, however, has some reflections feeling rain-soaked, imparting a glossy sheen that feels overly enthusiastic than the scene really calls for.

When it comes to performance, it's effectively a tie. Average FPS is within 1% of variance. Preset D is nominally 0.7 FPS ahead, which I'd chalk up to run-to-run variance, and I am quite confident stating that there is no performance penalty. Similarly, on 1% lows, the variance only came down to an imperceptible 1.47% on subsequent runs.

Metric

Preset F (DLSS 4.5 RR)

Preset D (DLSS 4.0 RR)

Variance (vs DLSS 4.0)

Average FPS

83.4

84.1

-0.8%

Average 1% low

61.4

62.3

-1.47%

Benchmark results can vary even on identical hardware due to silicon variance between GPUs and CPUs, system configuration, driver and background process variations, graphical presets, and ordinary run-to-run variance. The figures highlighted should therefore be treated as representative results from this test system rather than absolute performance figures.

Path tracing is slowly becoming a non-negotiable for me, and it wouldn't be possible without DLSS

Never thought I'd say this, but if it's got path tracing, I want it on.

17
By  Samarveer Singh

Alan Wake 2

Nvidia cracked the case for cleaner visuals with this one

Where the new ray-reconstruction model shone brightest in my own testing was Alan Wake 2. A specific scene that I picked in the "Mind Place" may as well be the quintessential example to confirm Nvidia's claims are not unfounded. With path tracing in the cabin, Preset F is undoubtedly more stable. The lamp clearly shows a bright emitter against a deep shadow with less shimmer and grain that are visible on Preset D around high-contrast edges. The path-traced bounce on the wooden bar top and the mounted antlers and brick behind it preserve better textures with Preset F, and the setting makes it obvious in juxtaposition.

Performance comparisons, similarly, give reasons to rejoice. In Alan Wake 2, the new Ray Reconstruction model led by 6% on average and 8% at 1% low, notably with lower PC latency too. This is consistent with the broader observations and testing around it, and reinforces that there are no concerns around performance penalties even with Ada Lovelace architecture. This was rather obvious as both Blackwell and Ada Lovelace are native FP8-capable architectures.

Metric

Preset F (DLSS 4.5 RR)

Preset D (DLSS 4.0 RR)

Variance (vs DLSS 4.0)

Average FPS

42.2

39.7

+6.3%

Average 1% low

37.2

34.5

+7.8%

Backrooms: Escape Together

Let's just say the nightmares are a lot more vivid now

At first, I thought Backrooms: Escape Together was a rather unlikely entrant to the DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction initial support list, but then I remembered that everything the game showcases is purpose-built to show off visual lighting, path tracing, and the entirety of the ray-reconstruction suite. The game makes a case for itself, needless to say, and this title shoehorned itself into the test.

That being said, it is challenging to create an apples-to-apples comparison. The game resets the level and respawns objects every time you run it, so my two captures don't contain the same puddles, lighting, or framing. The overall behavior, however, is evident. Preset F produces brighter, more vivid, more defined, and more stable reflections across the concrete, although it does bring back the over-wet look I noticed in Requiem. That's more justifiable in this title, though.

Performance, on the other hand, is another tie, which makes it a win for the second-gen RR. Preset F averaged 55.8 FPS against 54.8 FPS for D, while the 1% low settles at just 2.1%.

Metric

Preset F (DLSS 4.5 RR)

Preset D (DLSS 4.0 RR)

Variance (vs DLSS 4.0)

Average FPS

55.8

54.8

+1.8%

Average 1% low

24.3

23.8

+2.1%
DLSS 4.5 is expensive, but it’s the best thing to happen to my aging RTX PC

The upside is remarkable, but the cost isn't equal for all.

19
By  Samarveer Singh

Perhaps the most important upgrade to ray tracing in modern history is here

DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction reminds me what makes Nvidia such a formidable force in consumer graphics. Across the games, the second-gen AI denoiser delivered better reflections, cleaner visuals, and more stable path-traced imagery with no performance penalty, and in some cases, slightly better performance.

It is unreal that all of that is available to RTX owners for free now, which means this major leap in Ray Reconstruction is accessible to everyone who has purchased a GPU in the last eight years. Turns out, there absolutely is such a thing as a free lunch, and it's out now for RTX users.

Curious to see what this means for GPUs that aren't Blackwell-class, I put Preset F and Preset D head-to-head on my humble RTX 4070 Ti Super, testing both image quality and performance at 1440p across three games to see what Team Green has promised, and what they have delivered.

The test bench for the runs detailed below comprised of a GeForce RTX 4070 Ti Super coupled with a Ryzen 5 7600X, with 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory running with EXPO enabled.

Resident Evil Requiem

DLSS 4.5 RR brings a requiem for noisy reflections

Nvidia states that the new Ray Reconstruction model should bring better lighting accuracy, stronger temporal stability, and clearer detail in ray-traced scenes all while maintaining roughly the same performance as the preceding model. With Resident Evil Requiem, there are a couple of challenges involved in showing all of that off, though. Much of the game is characterized by dimmer lighting, matte concrete, and in a specific reflective scene that I captured under both presets, the two come quite close, barring the obvious clarity and crispiness in reflections.

Which is why I'd argue the gains become easier to spot when you put Preset F in front of reflections. Wet floors in the same dimly lit areas have more convincing color and reflection, and the lighting looks brighter and better defined. Pushing the brightness too far, in my testing, however, has some reflections feeling rain-soaked, imparting a glossy sheen that feels overly enthusiastic than the scene really calls for.

When it comes to performance, it's effectively a tie. Average FPS is within 1% of variance. Preset D is nominally 0.7 FPS ahead, which I'd chalk up to run-to-run variance, and I am quite confident stating that there is no performance penalty. Similarly, on 1% lows, the variance only came down to an imperceptible 1.47% on subsequent runs.

Alan Wake 2

Nvidia cracked the case for cleaner visuals with this one

Where the new ray-reconstruction model shone brightest in my own testing was Alan Wake 2. A specific scene that I picked in the "Mind Place" may as well be the quintessential example to confirm Nvidia's claims are not unfounded. With path tracing in the cabin, Preset F is undoubtedly more stable. The lamp clearly shows a bright emitter against a deep shadow with less shimmer and grain that are visible on Preset D around high-contrast edges. The path-traced bounce on the wooden bar top and the mounted antlers and brick behind it preserve better textures with Preset F, and the setting makes it obvious in juxtaposition.

Performance comparisons, similarly, give reasons to rejoice. In Alan Wake 2, the new Ray Reconstruction model led by 6% on average and 8% at 1% low, notably with lower PC latency too. This is consistent with the broader observations and testing around it, and reinforces that there are no concerns around performance penalties even with Ada Lovelace architecture. This was rather obvious as both Blackwell and Ada Lovelace are native FP8-capable architectures.

Backrooms: Escape Together

Let's just say the nightmares are a lot more vivid now

At first, I thought Backrooms: Escape Together was a rather unlikely entrant to the DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction initial support list, but then I remembered that everything the game showcases is purpose-built to show off visual lighting, path tracing, and the entirety of the ray-reconstruction suite. The game makes a case for itself, needless to say, and this title shoehorned itself into the test.

That being said, it is challenging to create an apples-to-apples comparison. The game resets the level and respawns objects every time you run it, so my two captures don't contain the same puddles, lighting, or framing. The overall behavior, however, is evident. Preset F produces brighter, more vivid, more defined, and more stable reflections across the concrete, although it does bring back the over-wet look I noticed in Requiem. That's more justifiable in this title, though.

Performance, on the other hand, is another tie, which makes it a win for the second-gen RR. Preset F averaged 55.8 FPS against 54.8 FPS for D, while the 1% low settles at just 2.1%.

Perhaps the most important upgrade to ray tracing in modern history is here

DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction reminds me what makes Nvidia such a formidable force in consumer graphics. Across the games, the second-gen AI denoiser delivered better reflections, cleaner visuals, and more stable path-traced imagery with no performance penalty, and in some cases, slightly better performance.

It is unreal that all of that is available to RTX owners for free now, which means this major leap in Ray Reconstruction is accessible to everyone who has purchased a GPU in the last eight years. Turns out, there absolutely is such a thing as a free lunch, and it's out now for RTX users.
